title: Characterization of Complex Systems Using the Design of Experiments Approach: Transient Protein Expression in Tobacco as a Case Study
protocol: Identify relevant factors and responses for inclusion in the design.
Define one or several responses for measurement.
Use available literature to select significant factors whose impact on the responses will be quantified.
Allocate the factor types (numeric or categoric).
Select ranges within which numeric factors will be varied during the DoE investigation.
Avoid using continuous variation for factors that cannot be adjusted precisely.
Select a number of discrete levels for factors with limited precision control.
Assign whether a categoric factor is nominal.
Select levels for both types of categoric factors.
Choose a useful base model.
Anticipate the relation between each factor and the response.
Consider factor interactions and their effect on the response.
Determine the number of levels for discrete numeric factors based on polynomial degree.
Ensure that the number of levels for discrete numeric factors is n + 1, where n is the polynomial degree.
Define the fraction of design space (FDS) for which prediction variance should be below a certain threshold.
Start DesignExpert and select "New Design".
In the "Response Surface" window, choose "Optimal".
Enter the number of numeric and categoric factors.
Enter factor names, units, types, sub-types, number of levels/level borders, and values for the levels.
Select "Best" under "Search" options.
Choose the desired "Optimality" criterion, here "D-optimal".
In the "Edit model…" menu, select a model that contains anticipated factors and interactions, or choose a full quadratic model if uncertain.
Select the number of "Blocks", using one block for consistency across experiments.
Balance the design.
Enable "Force categoric balance" in order to distribute the runs of the experiment evenly among the categoric factor levels.
Recalculate the design several times using the implemented random seed algorithm.
Adjust the number of runs for "Replicates" to ensure it is >5% of the number of "Model points".
Adjust the number of runs for "To estimate the lack of fit" to ensure it is >5% of the number of "Model points".
Continue to the next page and select the number of responses.
Enter the names and units of the selected responses.
Add additional responses at any time during data evaluation without any negative impact on the design.
Deselect terms in the base model that cannot be calculated based on the current number of levels.
Add a third level for the factor if necessary or remove the term from the model to ensure calculability.
Save the spreadsheet containing the optimal factor combinations once the calculation is complete.
Select the "Evaluation" sub-node and go to the "Graphs" tab in the "Design" node.
In the "Graphs tool", select "FDS".
Choose "Pred" as the error type in the "FDS Graph" box.
Enter the minimum detectable difference for "d".
Enter the approximate value for the estimated standard deviation of the system for "s".
Enter the alpha level suitable for the application, typically 0.05 (5%).
Ensure that the calculated FDS matches the percentage defined in section 1.3, typically >0.95.
Check if the FDS plot shows a flat curve indicating uniform prediction accuracy throughout the design space.
If the FDS is not satisfactory, go back to the "Design" node and select "Design Tools".
Choose "Augment Design…" and then choose "Augment".
Select the same "Search" and "Optimality" criteria as before.
Choose the same "Edit model" and "Force categoric balance" settings.
Change the "Put runs into block" setting to "Block1".
Enter the number of additional "Model points" in the "Runs" section.
Maintain at least 5% "Replicates" and "To estimate lack of fit" in the total design.
Reexamine the FDS graph after calculation completion.
Cultivate Escherichia coli in 5 ml LB medium containing ampicillin at 37 °C for 6-8 hours on an orbital shaker at 160 rpm.
Inoculate the LB medium with either 50 μl of liquid culture or transfer cells from colonies grown on plates using a pipette tip.
Follow the instructions in the DNA purification kit manual to purify pSo plasmid DNA and its derivatives from E. coli K12 strain DH5a.
Determine the DNA concentration in the purified eluate by measuring the absorbance of a 2 μl sample at 260 nm in a NanoDrop device.
Confirm the identity of the purified plasmid DNA by digestion with restriction endonucleases according to the plasmid sequence for unique and distinguishable fragment patterns.
Boil agarose in Tris-borate-EDTA (TBE) buffer to prepare 0.8-2.0% gels for DNA fragment separation.
Release the omega 5'UTR sequence from ~4 μg purified pSo DNA by treatment with EcoRI-HF and NcoI-HF REs in NEBuffer 4 at 37 °C for ~60 min.
Separate the fragments as described in sections 3.4.2 and 3.4.3.
Add 5 μl of five-fold sample buffer to 50 μl of the restriction enzyme-treated DNA sample.
Separate the DNA fragments by agarose gel electrophoresis at 100 V for ~40 min or until clear separation is achieved.
Include a lane containing DNA ladder size markers on each gel.
Isolate the larger fragment (pS) from the agarose gel using a gel extraction kit according to the manufacturer's manual.
Determine the concentration of the purified DNA as described in section 3.3).
Treat ~10 μg of each suitable donor vector with EcoRI-HF and NcoI-HF REs in NEBuffer 4 at 37 °C for ~60 min.
Separate the fragments as described in sections 3.4.2 and 3.4.3.
Purify the smaller 5'UTR-containing fragment as described in section 3.5.2.
Ligate isolated purified 5'UTRs to the isolated purified linear pS vector at 25 °C for 5 min according to the manufacturer's recommendations.
Use ~50 ng of vector DNA and a three-fold molar excess of 5'UTR DNA in a total volume of 20 μl.
Transform E coli cells with recombinant plasmids.
Add ~10 ng (~4-5 μl) of ligation mixture to 50 μl RbCl competent E. coli and mix gently.
Incubate the mixture on ice for 30-60 min.
Heat shock the mixture for 1.5 min at 42 °C and chill it on ice for 5-30 min.
Add 950 μl of antibiotic-free LB medium to the mixture.
Incubate the mixture for 1 hr at 37 °C and 160 rpm.
Spread 50 μl of the culture on LB agar plates containing ampicillin.
Spread 100 μl of the culture on additional LB agar plates containing ampicillin.
Incubate the plates for ~16-20 hours at 37 °C.
Inoculate 5-10 separate colonies representing each promoter-5'UTR ligation into 5-ml aliquots of LB medium containing ampicillin.
Purify the plasmid DNA.
Confirm the identity of the purified plasmid DNA.
Replace the 35SS promoter with the nos promoter in each of the four 5'UTR plasmids using AscI and EcoRI REs in NEBuffer 4 at 37 °C for 1 hr.
Add ~500 ng of purified plasmid DNA to 50 μl competent A. tumefaciens cells on ice.
Gently mix the cell-DNA mixture and transfer it into a prechilled 0.2 cm electroporation cuvette.
Pulse cells at 2.5 kV for 5 msec.
Add 950 μl of YEB medium without antibiotics to the electroporated cells.
Incubate the mixture for 2-4 hr at 26-28 °C and 160 rpm.
Spread 1-2 μl onto YEB agar plates containing antibiotics (50 mg/L carbenicillin, 25 mg/L kanamycin, 25 mg/L rifampicin) for the selection of transformants.
Inoculate three 5-ml aliquots of YEB medium containing antibiotics with cells from separate colonies representing each promoter-5'UTR ligation.
Incubate the inoculated medium at 26-28 °C and 160 rpm for 48-72 hours.
Transfer 2 μl of each incubated aliquot to separate 48 μl aliquots of PCR mastermix.

Amplify the expression cassette of each plasmid using appropriate primers under the conditions: initial denaturation at 94 °C, followed by 30 cycles of 94 °C for 15 sec, 51 °C for 30 sec and 72 °C for 120 sec, with a final elongation step at 72 °C for 8 min.
Determine the size of the PCR products by agarose gel electrophoresis.

Prepare A. tumefaciens glycerol stocks by mixing 500 μl 50% (v/v) sterile glycerol with 500 μl of A. tumefaciens cultures from section 3.8.6 for which transformation has been confirmed in section 3.9.3.
Store the glycerol stocks at -80 °C until further use.
Calculate the folding energies of different mRNAs using the RNAfold webserver.
Select "minimum free energy (MFE) and partition function" and "avoid isolated base pairs" options.
Choose "dangling energies on both sides of a helix in any case", "RNA parameters (Turner model, 2004)" and set "rescale energy parameters to given temperature (C)" to 25 °C.
Extract the "free energy of the thermodynamic ensemble" and the "frequency of the MFE structure in the ensemble" values for comparison.
Prepare a 0.1% solution of the fertilizer Ferty 2 Mega in de-ionized water at pH 5.9.
Flush 10 x 10 x 8 cm rockwool blocks extensively with deionized water to remove residual chemicals and equilibrate with fertilizer.
Place 1-2 tobacco seeds on each rockwool block followed by a short flush with fertilizer, being careful not to wash the seeds away.
Germinate and cultivate tobacco plants for 42 days in a greenhouse at 25/22 °C day/night temperature, 70% relative humidity, and a 16-hr photoperiod (180 mmol sec-1 m-2; λ = 400-700 nm).
Irrigate with fertilizer for 15 min every hour during the photoperiod in hydroponic culture.
Inoculate 5-50 ml of YEB medium containing antibiotics with 1% A. tumefaciens cryo-stock culture and incubate at 27 °C until the OD600nm reaches 5.0 (~48-72 hr depending on volume and vessel type).
Dilute the A. tumefaciens culture with water and 2-fold infiltration medium to match the OD600nm required for injection.
Confirm the OD600nm just before injection.
Select and label noncotyledon leaves and positions thereon to be treated according to a DoE strategy.
Do not inject different A. tumefaciens solutions into the same intercostal field.
Use opposing sections on each side of the mid-vein axis if more than two different solutions need to be injected at the same position, use an additional plant.
Thoroughly shake the A. tumefaciens solution to resuspend any cells that may have settled since preparing the dilution.
Aspirate the A. tumefaciens solution into a 1-ml syringe.
Gently scratch the epidermis at the intended injection position with a pipette tip or similar tool to facilitate influx of the A. tumefaciens solution.
Hold the syringe perpendicular to the leaf blade, touching the barrel against the intercostal field to be treated.
Gently push the outlet (with no needle attached) onto the bottom side of the leaf.
Press the top side of the leaf gently at the same time to prevent the leaf blade from shifting or rupturing.
Gently push down the syringe piston.
Ensure the A. tumefaciens solution enters the intercellular spaces within the leaf blade, causing treated areas to appear darker green and moist.
Repeat the procedure at several positions until the whole intercostal field is infiltrated with A. tumefaciens.
Maintain the syringe perpendicular to the leaf during injection.
Remove any excess bacterial suspension remaining on the underside of the leaf before applying a different solution if necessary.
Prepare a phytotron for treated plants approximately 24 hours before injection.
Transfer plants into the prepared phytotron after injection.
Place plants in trays large enough to allow irrigation with water until the end of the incubation period as determined by the DoE.
Establish a 16-hour photoperiod using six Osram cool white 36 W fluorescent tubes per 0.7 m² (75 mmol sec⁻¹ m⁻²; λ = 400-700 nm).
Limit the number of plants to six per 0.7 m² to prevent shading.
Ensure the correct intercostal field was selected by comparing labels from section 5.2.1 and the DoE plan before sampling.
Use a cork borer to remove 4-5 leaf discs from the treated intercostal fields at specified positions and times.
Stabilize the leaf with a hand-held paper towel while removing the discs to prevent rupture.
Determine the mass of each sample.
Place the sample in a 1.5 ml plastic reaction tube labeled with the sample name and mass.
Store the samples at -20 °C or -80 °C before protein quantitation.
Add 3 ml of extraction buffer per mg of sample mass to extract proteins.
Grind leaf discs using an electric pestle until no large fragments remain, avoiding overheating.
Centrifuge the sample twice at 16,000 x g for 20 min at 4 °C.
Transfer the supernatant into a clean 1.5 ml reaction tube after each step without disturbing the pellet.
Freeze the plant extracts at -20 °C or -80 °C if pausing the process for several months.
Confirm that a freeze-thaw cycle does not affect the concentration of target proteins.
Measure the DsRed fluorescence.
Prepare three technical replicates of each sample into black 96-well half-area plates (50 μl extract per well).
Avoid formation of bubbles during pipetting.
Use six dilutions (0, 25, 75, 125, 175 and 225 μg/ml) of a DsRed standard per 96-well plate to generate a linear reference curve.
Prepare the dilutions in PBS.
Store the dilutions at 4 °C for use within 3 months.
Measure fluorescence twice sequentially in a 96-well plate reader fitted with 530/25 nm excitation and 590/35 nm emission filters.
Average the fluorescence over the two reads and the three technical replicates for each sample.
Subtract the value recorded for the blank control containing 0 μg/ml DsRed from each read.
Use these blank-corrected values to perform a linear regression yielding a reference curve (through the origin of ordinates).
Determine the slope of the reference curve.
Convert the fluorescence measured for the samples into DsRed concentrations using the slope of the reference curve.
If necessary, dilute the samples so that the readout falls within the concentration interval of the standards.
Consider this dilution factor in subsequent calculations.
Determine the concentration of 2G12.
Prepare a surface plasmon resonance (SPR) device.
Couple Protein A to the activated surface of one flow cell.
Inactivate the surface without coupling of Protein A in another flow cell as reference.
Dilute plant extracts 1:20 in SPR running buffer.
Measure response units (RU) of antibody binding to Protein A in three technical replicates at the end of a 90 μl injection.
Subtract RU measured at the reference flow cell from the RU measured in the experimental flow cell.
Measure a 585 ng/ml 2G12 standard after each 10-15 samples.
Subtract the value measured in the reference flow cells for the 2G12 standards.
Use the average RU of these standards to calculate a linear reference curve through the origin of ordinates.
Calculate the 2G12 concentrations in the samples based on the 1:20 dilution and the slope of the reference curve.
Manually analyze the responses observed in expression experiments for extreme values indicating measurement errors.
Analyze unusual results from factor combinations that generate unanticipated responses.
Identify missing values in the data set.
Transfer analyzed response data into the "Design" node of DesignExpert.
Ensure response data are correctly assigned to corresponding factor settings.
Choose a response to be analyzed and initially select "none" in the transformation tab.
Consider applying a transformation if the min/max ratio of the response is larger than 10.
Obtain the most useful transformation from the Box-Cox plot in the "Diagnostics" tab.
Use a Log10 transformation when appropriate.
Proceed to the "Fit summary" tab for general information on important factors.
Edit the initial model based on significance using the automated mode.
Select a process order that is one order above the suggested model.
Choose "Backward" in the "Selection" field.
Iteratively remove nonsignificant terms from the model after proceeding to the "ANOVA" tab based on the "Alpha out" value of 0.100.
Automatically correct the model hierarchy when prompted by the software.
Switch back to the "Model" tab if necessary.
Change "Selection" to "Manual".
Eliminate factors with p-values above a predefined threshold (here 0.05).
Remove factors unlikely based on mechanistic considerations.
Evaluate the refreshed model in terms of the p-value of the "Model".
Assess the "Lack-of-fit" value for significance.
Check values for "R-squared", "Adjusted R-squared", and "Predicted R-squared".
Compare these values for different models including/excluding factors at several significance levels.
Ensure the points are randomly scattered within the limits in the "Residuals vs. Predicted" chart.
Investigate whether the points in the "Residuals vs. run" chart scatter randomly within the limits.
Use block building to counteract a trend in the data if a pattern such as a "stairway" is observed in the "Residuals vs. run" chart.
Look for a straight diagonal line in the "Predicted vs. Actual" plot.
Check for an overlap of the blue and green vertical lines in the Box-Cox-plot.
If the green line does not match the blue one, go back to section 7.3 and improve the model building round by selecting the data transformation suggested by the Box-Cox-plot.
Ensure that the points in the "Residuals vs. Factor" charts scatter randomly within the limits.
Check for curvature in the data distribution, which may indicate a missing factor in the model.
Make sure there is random scattering of the data within the limits in the "Externally studentized residuals", "Leverage", "DFFITS" and "DFBETAS" plots.
Ensure an evenly low distribution without extreme values in the "Cook's Distance" plot.
Visualize the evaluated model in the "Model graphs" tab.
For a limited number of numeric factors, use the response surface ("3D surface") representation to assess optima/characteristics manually.
Use this prediction for all settings to be evaluated.
Export the predicted values and compile them into a data array.
Normalize the expression data based on leaf masses to yield specific expression levels or rates.
Alternatively, export coefficients from the "ANOVA" tab into a spreadsheet.
Multiply these coefficients with an array of factor settings to generate the same data array.
Conduct confirmation experiments for model points of major interest.
Perform transient protein expression under conditions selected for point prediction.
Determine protein concentrations for this experiment as described previously.
Check whether the average protein concentration in the confirmation experiment falls within the prediction interval of the response surface model obtained during point prediction.
A match affirms the predictive power of the model.
A mismatch indicates a low model quality and additional runs can be required.
